analysis.investment_thesis: IIFL Capital Services is a well-run capital markets franchise with impressive ROE (31.6%) and revenue CAGR (15.3%), but the critically low promoter holding of 30.93% and rising debt (₹1,742 Cr borrowings in 2025) disqualify it under my framework. The inherently cyclical broking business produces volatile cash flows — negative OCF in 2 of last 5 years — which is the antithesis of the steady compounders I seek.
key_strengths: Excellent capital returns: ROE 31.6% and ROCE 33.3% are well above my 18-22% target, showing a high-quality operating franchise
Reasonable valuation: P/E of 17x sits within my acceptable 12-20x band given strong earnings trajectory (net profit CAGR 21.6% over 7 years)
Strong operating margins: 38% operating margin with growing profit (₹250 Cr in 2023 to ₹713 Cr in 2025) reflects operating leverage in the model
key_risks: Dangerously low promoter stake: 30.93% is far below my 55% minimum — no meaningful skin in the game raises serious alignment and governance concerns
Debt/Equity of 0.62 breaches my 0.5 hard ceiling, with borrowings nearly tripling from ₹607 Cr (2022) to ₹1,742 Cr (2025) — aggressive leverage expansion is unacceptable
Highly cyclical, capital-markets-dependent revenue: negative OCF in 2023 (-₹793 Cr) and 2024 (-₹118 Cr) shows this is not the predictable, recession-resistant business I require
red_flags: Promoter holding at 30.93% — deeply below my 55% threshold; this is a deal-breaker
Borrowings surged 3x in 3 years (₹607 Cr → ₹1,742 Cr), funded by debt rather than retained earnings
OCF swung from +₹795 Cr (2022) to -₹793 Cr (2023) in a single year — hallmark of a cyclical business, not a compounder
Capital markets broking faces structural disruption from zero-commission discount brokers (Zerodha, Upstox) — pricing power is under permanent pressure
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my perspective, IIFL Capital Services operates a genuinely competent capital markets business — the ROE of 31.6% and ROCE of 33.3% are hard to dismiss, and a revenue CAGR of 15.3% over seven years is solid. But the business that produced those numbers is a cyclical broking franchise, not a stable consumer compounder. Revenue fell from ₹933 Cr (2018) to ₹758 Cr (2020) and operating cash flow swung by ₹1,588 Cr between 2022 and 2023. I built DMart on businesses where I could predict demand five years forward with reasonable confidence — capital markets volumes are the opposite of that.

The two structural disqualifiers here are the promoter stake and the balance sheet. At 30.93%, promoters hold less than a third of the company — well below my non-negotiable 55% floor. When promoters don't own enough to feel real pain, capital allocation discipline tends to soften over time. Meanwhile, borrowings have jumped from ₹292 Cr in 2021 to ₹1,742 Cr in 2025, pushing D/E to 0.62. In my experience, financial services companies that grow leverage quickly during bull markets are precisely the ones that get hurt most in downturns. The P/E at 17x is fair, not cheap, and I would need a much larger margin of safety to compensate for the cyclicality and governance concerns here.
